text.p: Den norske Bank ASA (DNB), Norway's top commercial bank, said on Wednesday that cost cuts and a healthy national economy helped lift 1996 net profits by 1.7 percent.
The earnings rose to 2.70 billion crowns ($408.9 million) from 2.66 billion in 1995, corresponding to earnings per share of 4.22 crowns and a 20 percent return on equity, DnB said in a statement.
The board of directors proposed a dividend of 1.75 crowns per share, up from 1.5 crowns in 1995.

"The strong results reflect sound operations, reduced costs and a healthy trend in the Norwegian economy," group managing director Finn Hvistendahl said in a statement. "This has coincided with a favourable loan-loss trend and continued reversals on previous loan losses."

The volume of new loan losses was 837 million crowns in 1996, down from 1.25 billion in the previous year. Net reversals -- or writebacks on bad loans turned good -- fell to 380 million crowns from 479 million.
DnB stock jumped 3.25 percent to 28.60 crowns on the Oslo Bourse in afternoon trade following the announcement.
DnB is 52-percent owned by the Norwegian government, which bailed out major banks of a financial crisis in the early 1990s.
Analysts agreed that a fight DnB has with tax authorities over tax losses-carried forward from the crisis years was putting a questionmark over the bank's future net earnings.
"The extra 0.25 crowns in dividend was a positive surprise but the question is if it is sustainable," said bank analyst James Alexander of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.
"When they start paying taxes and normal provisions I have them earning three crowns per share, which would mean a sustainable level of 1.5 crowns in dividend," he said.
The 1996 accounts include a tax charge of 22 million crowns, up from six million in 1995. If the taxman had his way, DnB would have paid 617 million crowns in taxes in 1996, the bank said.
"DnB has a complicated tax situation," said Alexander, who had the share on hold. "It probably won't start paying normal taxes until in 1998."
Hvistendahl said growth in lending and deposits almost compensated for the pressure on interest margins, which dropped to an annual 2.30 percent from 2.51 percent in 1995.
Net interest income, the bank's core business, fell to 4.24 billion from 4.35 billion. Other operating income also dropped in 1996, to 2.67 billion from 2.77 billion crowns.
However, operating expenses shrank to 4.60 billion crowns from 4.94 billion to help improve the overall result, which largerly met market expectations.
Operating profits came to 2.72 billion crowns, up 61 million from 1995. Pre-tax profits before loan losses were 2.34 billion crowns, compared with 2.20 billion crowns the year before.
Salomon Brothers said in a market update on Monday that DnB and Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse, the country's second largest bank, remained attractive on price/book and relative yield valuations.
Christiania, which also has a tax fight on its hands, will present annual results on February 19.
